source: Spearman (1904) General intelligence, objectively determined and measured
finding: Spearman set up four experimental series on English school children and tested whether sensory discrimination (light, weight, pitch) tracks school cleverness. He corrected for measurement error and for age and sex.
numbers: Series I: 24 oldest children of a Berkshire village school (Light, Weight, Sound). Series II: next 36 oldest children, sound only, tested collectively (about 1.5 hours). Series IV used regular school exams and pitch.
limits: Small samples, rough error corrections. Series II raw correlation was -0.25 and flipped after age was removed, a warning about irrelevant factors.
agent_relevance: Shows the founding method: correct for noise, remove nuisance variables, then ask what is common. Our agent benchmarks need the same noise correction.

source: Spearman (1904) General intelligence, objectively determined and measured
finding: In Series IV, pitch discrimination correlated with school studies once errors were removed. The order of subjects matched their rank in general ability.
numbers: Corrected average correlation with the four school studies 0.78 (observed 0.57): Classics 0.89, French 0.88, English 0.73, Mathematics 0.61. With total school ability: raw 0.68, corrected 0.87 (school orders correlated 0.95 with each other).
limits: Earlier series used arbitrary assumed reliabilities. Spearman himself called parts of the argument rough.
agent_relevance: Which tasks sit highest on g depends on the corrections; raw task scores understate it.

source: Spearman (1904) General intelligence, objectively determined and measured
finding: Core claim: general discrimination and general intelligence are the same thing once errors are removed. Spearman gets a correlation of about 1.00 by two routes.
numbers: Village school: nine cross-correlations averaged 0.38; the intellective gradings correlate 0.55 with each other and the discrimination gradings 0.25. Empirical route: amalgamated lists correlate 0.66, giving a true correlation near 1.00 (another check 0.96; a music-school check 0.72 raw, again 1.00).
limits: Rests on correction for attenuation with N = 24 pupils. Later work did not find a correlation of 1.0 between sensory discrimination and g.
agent_relevance: A very high reported factor correlation can be an artifact of the correction. Treat claims that one task equals g with suspicion.

source: Spearman (1904) General intelligence, objectively determined and measured
finding: Law of the Universal Unity of the Intellective Function: every branch of intellectual activity shares one common function plus a specific part unique to it.
numbers: Tested on twelve random pairs of test groups: mean correlation of the common elements 'precisely 1.00' with mean deviation 0.05. For dissimilar groups the commons overlap only 0.86 (74%), leaving 26% specific.
quote: Whenever branches of intellectual activity are at all dissimilar, then their correlations with one another appear wholly due to their being all variously saturated
limits: Spearman says it needs 'a much vaster corroborative basis'. Cannot rule out several group factors.
agent_relevance: Original two-factor statement: score = general part + task-specific part. This is the model behind all later LLM g-factor papers.

source: Spearman (1904) General intelligence, objectively determined and measured
finding: The Hierarchy of the Intelligences: correlations between faculties fall in the same rank order moving away from the most g-saturated subject. This is the early form of the tetrad pattern.
numbers: Table of observed correlations, probable errors about 0.01 for school studies and about 0.03 for music; order Classics, French, English, Mathematics, Pitch, Music held in nearly every cell. Spearman called the uniformity 'very nearly perfect'.
limits: Group-factor models (Thurstone 1938) show the same pattern can arise from several correlated factors; the tetrad test is weak at telling them apart.
agent_relevance: Tasks have a g-loading that predicts how well they relate to others. We could rank our problem classes by loading.

source: Spearman (1904) General intelligence, objectively determined and measured
finding: Spearman reviewed Wissler's null result between mental tests and class standing and explained it by low reliability and restricted range, not absence of g.
numbers: Wissler's tests correlated 0.06 with intelligence and 0.09 among themselves; Spearman's recomputation of Gilbert's data (about 1,100 children) gave an average 0.19 (+/-0.04) for general ability vs sensory discrimination.
limits: Attenuation explanation is untestable without reliabilities; Wissler's sample was mostly college students (range restriction).
agent_relevance: Failure to find a common factor can come from noisy or range-restricted items; check item reliability before concluding a task is independent.

source: Spearman (1904) review chapters I-IV: earlier mental test studies
finding: Spearman reviewed the 1890s experimental literature. Most studies found weak or no correlation between simple tests and intelligence, which he blamed on poor method.
numbers: Samples cited: Gilbert about 1,200 children (1893); Seashore about 200 children aged 6-15; Bagley 160 children (reaction time unrelated to school intelligence); Kirkpatrick about 500 children; Binet 11 selected children (5 cleverest and 6 dullest of a class of 32).
limits: Narrative review, no pooled estimate.
agent_relevance: One benchmark rarely predicts another; only multi-test batteries expose the common factor.

source: Wikipedia: G factor (psychometrics) (secondary summary of Spearman, Thurstone, Jensen, Detterman)
finding: Secondary summary: g typically accounts for 40-50% of test variance, loadings always positive, mean about .60.
numbers: g loadings .10 to .90 (mean about .60, SD about .15); Raven's matrices about .80; Wechsler full-scale IQ vs g factor scores > .95. Spearman's six-subject example loadings from .958 (Classics) to .646 (Music). Thurstone 1938: seven primary mental abilities.
limits: Wikipedia page, not primary. Sample sizes missing for several studies.
agent_relevance: Gives the human baselines (40-50% variance, mean r about .45-.50) that LLM papers compare against.

source: Johnson, te Nijenhuis, Bouchard et al. (g across test batteries), as summarized in Wikipedia: G factor
finding: Different test batteries measure nearly the same g.
numbers: g factors from different batteries correlated .95 to 1.00 for most pairs and .79 to .96 for the CFIT battery.
limits: Seen only through the secondary summary; Stankov objects that 'correlations between the g factors from different test batteries are not unity'. Original not opened.
agent_relevance: If different benchmark suites share one g, any good battery ranks models; verify with two suites.

source: Spearman's law of diminishing returns (Spearman 1927; Detterman & Daniel 1989; Tucker-Drob 2009; Blum & Holling), via Wikipedia: G factor
finding: g is weaker at high ability: test intercorrelations fall as ability rises.
numbers: Spearman 1927: mean r .466 in 78 normal children vs .782 in 22 defective children. Detterman & Daniel 1989: subtest r about .7 (IQ<78) vs about .4 (IQ>122). Tucker-Drob 2009: g about 75% of variance at very low IQ vs about 30% at very high IQ. Blum & Holling: a sample 2 SD higher has mean r about .15 lower.
limits: Secondary summary only; size varies by sample.
agent_relevance: Prediction for LLMs: as frontier models saturate, the benchmark positive manifold should weaken. Krakauer 2026 sees this.

source: Wikipedia: Cattell-Horn-Carroll theory
finding: CHC joins Cattell-Horn Gf-Gc with Carroll's three-stratum model: stratum I narrow abilities, II broad abilities, III g.
numbers: Carroll (1993) re-analysed 461 factor-analytic data sets in an 800-page book. Ten broad abilities: Gc, Gf, Gq, Grw, Gsm, Glr, Gv, Ga, Gs, Gt (Gt not assessed by any major IQ test). Horn by 1991 had 9-10 broad abilities. McGrew expanded CHC in the late 1990s.
limits: Secondary source. Horn rejected a single g while Carroll thought evidence for g 'overwhelming'. Cross-Battery Assessment built on CHC is criticised as statistically flawed.
agent_relevance: The broad-ability list (Gf, Gc, Gq, Grw, Gsm, Glr, Gv, Ga, Gs) is a ready vocabulary for classifying our problem classes.

source: Carroll (1993) Human Cognitive Abilities: A Survey of Factor-Analytic Studies
finding: Founding synthesis: hierarchical exploratory factor analysis of 461 data sets gives narrow abilities (stratum I), broad abilities (II) and g (III).
numbers: 461 data sets, 800 pages (both figures confirmed only through Wikipedia).
limits: Book not opened; narrow-ability count not verified here.
agent_relevance: Base taxonomy for CHC; Carroll thought the evidence for g overwhelming.

source: Wikipedia: Fluid and crystallized intelligence (Cattell, Horn)
finding: Cattell proposed fluid (Gf) and crystallized (Gc) intelligence. Gf peaks in the mid-20s and declines; Gc rises and stays stable to about 65.
numbers: Cattell introduces Gf/Gc (page gives 1943; 1963 'critical experiment'; Horn and Cattell age differences 1967). Gf peaks about age 27; Gc declines after about 65. Jaeggi et al. 2008: 70 people, dual n-back 25 min/day for 8-19 days raised matrix scores; later studies found no gain; a 2012 meta-analysis found no transfer.
limits: Secondary source; other sources date Cattell's proposal to 1941. Messick 1989 argued low Gf scores may reflect low interest.
agent_relevance: Gf is novel problem solving, Gc is stored knowledge. LLM benchmarks mostly measure Gc, which matters for what a scaffold can change.

source: Ilic & Gignac (2024) Evidence of interrelated cognitive-like capabilities in large language models: indications of artificial general intelligence or achievement?
finding: Factor analysis of 591 LLMs on 12 Hugging Face tests found a strong positive manifold and a general factor of artificial ability (AGA).
numbers: N = 591 models (from 3,862 after removing 85% near-duplicates); 12 tests mapped to Gf, Gkn, Grw, Gq. Mean inter-test r = 0.73 (0.35 to 0.99). g explains 65.6% of variance; mean g loading 0.81 (0.64 to 0.96); omega hierarchical 0.94; CFI .984, TLI .977, RMSEA .089, SRMR .025. Largest loading: a mathematics composite (0.96).
quote: We found evidence for a LLM test performance positive manifold, as well as an artificial general ability (AGA) factor.
limits: Tests are narrow (no spatial tests); high reliability (median .97) inflates g versus humans (40-50%, r .45-.50); authors call it achievement not intelligence. RMSEA above .08.
agent_relevance: LLM positive manifold is stronger than in humans, so one score ranks models well; it says little about which scaffold step helps which task.

source: Ilic & Gignac (2024), group-factor structure
finding: Only one combined reading/writing plus knowledge group factor appeared, not four. No independent Gf factor.
numbers: Two-factor EFA was unstable: Hellaswag loaded 1.07 and the two factors correlated 0.78. Winogrande and Hellaswag r = 0.95. Correlations of 0.85 to 0.91 between Grw and Gkn. No Gf factor separate from g.
limits: Gf proxies (e.g. Hellaswag) may be solved by memory of text; Gustafsson (2001) argues Gf is isomorphic with g in humans anyway.
agent_relevance: Consistent with LLM benchmarks being mostly crystallised knowledge. Fluid reasoning for our agent must be measured with novel tasks.

source: Ilic & Gignac (2024), parameters and g
finding: Parameter count predicts the general factor, with diminishing returns.
numbers: Parameters vs AGA, N = 577: Pearson r = 0.54 [0.48, 0.59], Spearman 0.62. Grw/Gkn: Pearson 0.11 [0.05, 0.18], Spearman 0.42. Cubic spline beat linear (F(2,573) = 27.93, eta2 = .063; Grw/Gkn F = 87.13, eta2 = .230). AGA rises to about 10 B parameters, flat 10-20 B, slow gain to 80 B. Only 10 models above 80 B.
limits: Only 10 very large models; no data on training tokens, so size is confounded.
agent_relevance: Size explains only about 30% of g scores, so scaffolds and training matter as well.

source: Burnell, Hao, Conway & Hernandez-Orallo (2023) Revealing the structure of language model capabilities
finding: A factor analysis of HELM data found three factors, not one: reasoning, comprehension and core language modelling.
numbers: 29 LLMs x 27 tasks. Hull method chose 3 factors. Frequentist EFA (oblimin): 33%, 31%, 17% variance, 82% cumulative. Mean task correlation r = 0.56 (median 0.6). Factors correlate moderately (reasoning with comprehension 0.51 [0.19, 0.73], with language modelling 0.49). Fit poor (CFI 0.70, TLI 0.61, RMSEA 0.26), so a Bayesian EFA was added and agreed.
limits: Tiny sample (29 models, mostly 2022 GPT-3 family); poor fit; factor names assigned by one cognitive scientist.
agent_relevance: Argues LLM ability is not monolithic; improving one factor may hurt another.

source: Burnell et al. (2023), model properties
finding: Size, instruction tuning and training length relate differently to the three factors.
numbers: Log model size correlates 0.70 [0.46, 0.85] with comprehension, -0.50 [-0.72, -0.17] with language modelling, 0.08 [-0.38, 0.52] with reasoning. Instruction tuning vs comprehension 0.23 [-0.13, 0.54]. Training tokens vs comprehension -0.02 [-0.47, 0.44]. InstructGPT davinci-002 scored 3.58 on reasoning vs about 1 for most others.
limits: Wide CIs; the only large instruction-tuned, RLHF-trained models were from one lab, so tuning is confounded.
agent_relevance: Reasoning tracks tuning more than size, so a scaffold effect is plausible.

source: Maimon, Cohen, Vishne, Ravfogel & Tsarfaty (2026) From Benchmarks to Skills: Low-Rank Factors for LLM Evaluation
finding: A 60 x 44 model-by-benchmark matrix is low-rank. Eight latent skills were recovered by principal axis factoring with varimax.
numbers: 60 LLMs (2B to 27B plus proprietary) x 44 benchmarks; C = 8 factors, chosen by Kaiser's rule and an 85% cumulative-variance threshold. Factor 1 is general NLU. Saturated easy tasks (SST-2, MNLI) compress into Factor 1; harder tasks (MedQA, LegalBench) form separate axes.
limits: Eight factors, so the paper's own result differs from single-g claims. Only three prompts per task.
agent_relevance: A skill-profile view could route a problem class to a scaffold. Skills include summarisation, retrieval, quantitative precision.

source: Maimon et al. (2026), robustness checks
finding: The 8-factor space is stable under perturbation; PCA gives a worse, less useful representation than principal axis factoring.
numbers: Under-extraction (k = 6, 7) merged skills (principal angles 43-60 degrees); over-extraction (k = 9, 10) added redundant axes while the eight core factors rotated at most 26 degrees. Removing 30% of models left factors stable; Tucker congruence >= 0.90 counts as similar.
limits: Prompt averaging may weaken correlations for prompt-sensitive tasks. Factor labels written by GPT-4o and DeepSeek-R1.
agent_relevance: Method to find redundant benchmarks: tasks with high shared variance can be dropped from our evaluation set.

source: Maimon et al. (2026), what drives factor scores
finding: Tasks with wide score spread across models shape factors most; model diversity is needed to reveal structure.
numbers: Phi-4 leads factor 7 (Faithful Summarization and Quantitative Precision) at about +2.5 SD; every model above +1.5 SD was trained on textbook-quality synthetic math and logic chains.
limits: Stories about training data are post hoc.
agent_relevance: Training data style can move one factor without moving others, so a scaffold gain on one skill need not carry over.

source: Haznitrama, Ardi & Oh (2026) A Neuropsychologically Grounded Evaluation of LLM Cognitive Abilities (NeuroCognition)
finding: Factor analysis of 156 models on 10 benchmarks gave a single general factor: 75% of variance, all loadings above 0.76.
numbers: Principal axis factoring, N = 156 models (Artificial Analysis); parallel analysis supports one factor (PA1) = 75% of total variance; every loading > 0.76.
limits: Authors note this also shows benchmark redundancy. Only 10 standard benchmarks, no spatial or memory tasks.
agent_relevance: Confirms Ilic & Gignac with newer models. Standard benchmarks agree with each other, so they cannot tell abilities apart.

source: Haznitrama et al. (2026), NeuroCognition vs g
finding: Adapted neuropsychological tests (Raven's matrices, spatial working memory, Wisconsin Card Sort) correlate with general capability but add distinct signal.
numbers: NeuroCognition average vs 11-benchmark average r = .86 (p = .001, N = 10). RAPM image version vs ARC-AGI-2 r = .87 (p = .024, N = 6), but ARC-AGI-2 vs the general benchmark average r = .09. Task Interference benchmark r = .24 (N = 10).
limits: N is 6 to 10 models, so correlations are fragile. Humans and LLMs fail on different parts of the same tasks.
agent_relevance: Fluid-like tests on novel images seem to separate from the general factor, matching Gf vs Gc. Test the scaffold on such tasks.

source: Krakauer (2026) The Rise and Fall of G in AGI
finding: PCA on a model-by-benchmark-by-time matrix shows a very strong positive manifold that weakens when reasoning models arrive in 2024.
numbers: 39 models (2019-2025), 14 benchmarks; all 28 pairwise correlations positive on 8 benchmarks. PC1 = 90% of variance on a 5-benchmark core battery (MMLU, GSM8K, MATH, HumanEval, GPQA Diamond; n = 19), 77% by 2024. 4-benchmark battery: PC1 peaks at 92% in 2023-24 then falls to 64%; second eigenvalue rises to 1.88; effective dimensionality up 40% to 1.9.
limits: Preliminary; small n per epoch; benchmark choice drives results; no confidence intervals seen in the text read.
agent_relevance: Inference-time reasoning (like our scaffold) adds a second dimension beyond g. Fits the law of diminishing returns.

source: Krakauer (2026), eigenvector rotation
finding: The direction of g rotates as models outsource reasoning to tools.
numbers: 5-benchmark battery: 6.4 degree rotation when DeepSeek V3 enters; leave-one-out check: three models exceed 3 degrees (DeepSeek V3 5.58, GPT-4 3.35, DeepSeek R1 3.16). Epoch IV (from Sept 2024) has a second eigenvalue.
limits: Rotation analysis on few models; author calls results preliminary.
agent_relevance: 'AI-hedgehog' (one g) vs 'AI-foxes' (specialists): our agent mixes a general model with tools, so expect task-specific profiles.

source: Krakauer (2026), relation to Ilic & Gignac
finding: Krakauer restates that Ilic and Gignac found about 66% g and argued LLMs show Artificial General Achievement that fits crystallised intelligence, with little evidence of fluid intelligence.
numbers: 12 benchmarks in four broad-ability categories; g about 66% of variance; human g typically 40-60% (Jensen 1998, Carroll 1993).
limits: Secondary restatement. The point that g means correlation among abilities, not breadth, is the author's own argument.
agent_relevance: 'General' here means correlated, not broad. Do not cite a g factor as evidence of general reasoning.

source: Cross-study comparison of LLM factor structures (Ilic & Gignac; Burnell; Maimon; Haznitrama)
finding: The general factor is large in all LLM studies but the structure is not agreed: 1 factor (75%, Haznitrama), 1 factor plus combined Grw/Gkn (66%, Ilic), 3 factors (82% cumulative, Burnell), 8 factors (Maimon).
numbers: Human reference: g 40-50% of variance, mean inter-test r .45-.50, omega hierarchical high .80s; LLM omega hierarchical .94. Samples 156, 591, 29 and 60 models.
limits: Samples and test sets differ, so numbers are not comparable.
agent_relevance: Build the schema on problem classes, not on an assumed single skill.
